title: ASIC chair puts insurance pricing and claims basics ahead of enforcement priorities
full_text:
ASIC chair Sarah Court (pictured) has warned insurers, banks and super funds that failures on basic customer obligations will remain in the regulator’s sights.
She named premium calculation and claims handling alongside newer risks such as artificial intelligence.
Opening the ASIC Annual Forum in Sydney on Tuesday, her first as chair, Court said the regulator continued to see institutions in banking, insurance and superannuation falling short on fundamentals. Interest rates and premiums must be calculated correctly, she said. Customers in hardship must get the support the law requires, and legitimate insurance claims and superannuation death benefits must be handled properly and without unnecessary delay.
“These are not peripheral obligations,” said Court.
She said neither complexity, innovation nor the pace of change reduced those obligations.
Court also signalled closer attention to how firms manage outsourced services. She said the financial system increasingly depends on a small number of critical technology and service providers, and that a serious failure at one could affect several institutions. Relying on a third party, she said, does not remove a firm’s responsibility for the service or its consequences.
On artificial intelligence, Court said it could improve productivity but was also making false material more convincing and scams easier to run at scale. Firms must protect customers from technology-enabled harm and remain accountable when automated systems affect outcomes, she said.
Court also said ASIC is strengthening how it assesses reports of misconduct alongside its surveillance and market data, to spot developing patterns earlier.
Court will announce ASIC’s enforcement priorities for 2027 on Wednesday. She said they would focus on emerging risks, but that ASIC remained equally focused on persistent failures to get the basics right.
The speech gives a clear indication of where insurers are likely to sit in tomorrow’s priorities. Premium calculation errors and claims delays have been repeated sources of remediation and code breaches. This month alone, the Life Code Compliance Committee sanctioned an insurer that underpaid 66 claims by about $1.6 million.
Court’s comments on outsourcing are also relevant to the general insurance market, where claims handling, assessing and repairs are often delegated to third parties. Her message was that a firm owns the outcome even when a contractor delivers it.
That principle extends to brokers and underwriting agencies working within delegated authority arrangements. Firms should expect ASIC to test whether their oversight of those arrangements works in practice.
author: Josh Recamara
